exampleAnswers.title: Finding a Parametrization of a Surface of Revolution: Rotation About the x-Axis

question.text: The vector-valued function $\mathbf{r}(x,\theta)$ parametrizes the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $y=\sqrt{1-x^2}$ by $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis for $x \in [-1,1].$ Which of the following could be $\mathbf{r}?$
question.explanation:
A point $(x,y,z)$ on the surface generated by rotating the graph of $y=f(x)$ by $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis for $x\in[a,b] $ has the position vector

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r} = \big\langle x, \: f(x) \cos\theta, \: f(x) \sin\theta \big\rangle, \quad x\in[a,b], \quad \theta\in [0,2\pi). \end{align*}

First, notice that $y=f(x) =\sqrt{1-x^2} \ge 0$ for all $x \in [-1,1].$

So, the parametrization of our surface of revolution is

\[ \mathbf{r}(x,\theta) = \big\langle x, \: \sqrt{1-x^2} \cos\theta, \: \sqrt{1-x^2} \sin\theta \big\rangle, \quad x \in [-1,1], \quad \theta \in [0,2\pi). \]

question.text:
\[ \mathbf r(x, \theta) = \big\langle x, \: \tan{x} \cos\theta, \: \textrm{_______} \big \rangle \]

The vector-valued function $\mathbf{r}(x,\theta)$ above parametrizes the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $y=\tan{x}$ by $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis for $x \in \Big[0,\dfrac{\pi}{4} \Big].$ What is the third component of $\mathbf{r}?$
question.explanation:
A point $(x,y,z)$ on the surface generated by rotating the graph of $y=f(x)$ by $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis for $x\in[a,b] $ has the position vector

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r} = \big\langle x, \: f(x) \cos\theta, \: f(x) \sin\theta \big\rangle, \quad x\in[a,b], \quad \theta\in [0,2\pi). \end{align*}

First, notice that $y=f(x) = \tan{x} \geq 0$ for all $x \in \Big[0,\dfrac{\pi}{4} \Big].$

So, the parametrization of our surface of revolution is

\[ \mathbf{r}(x,\theta) = \big\langle x, \: \tan{x} \cos\theta, \: {\color{blue}{\tan{x} \sin\theta}} \big\rangle, \quad x \in \Big[0,\dfrac{\pi}{4} \Big], \quad \theta \in [0,2\pi). \]

Therefore, the third component of $\mathbf r$ is ${\color{blue}{\tan{x} \sin\theta}}.$

exampleAnswers.title: The Fundamental Vector Product of a Surface of Revolution

question.text:
\[ \big\langle \text{_______}\,, \: -x^2 \cos\theta, \: -x^2\sin\theta \big\rangle \]

The fundamental vector product of the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $y=x^2$ by $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis for $x \in [0,1]$ is given above. What is the $1$st component of the product?
question.explanation:
Notice that $y=x^2\geq 0$ for all $x \in [0,1].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r} = \big\langle x, f(x) \cos\theta, \: f(x) \sin\theta \big\rangle, \qquad (x,\theta) \in D \end{align*}

where $f(x)=x^2,$ and

\[ D = \big\{ (x,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \: 0 \leq \theta \lt 2\pi \big\}. \]

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_x &= \bigg\langle \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial x}, \: \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial x}, \: \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x} \bigg\rangle = \big\langle 1, \: f' \cos\theta, \: f' \sin\theta \big\rangle \\[10pt] \mathbf{r}'_\theta &= \bigg\langle \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial \theta}, \: \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial \theta}, \: \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial \theta} \bigg\rangle = \big\langle 0, \: -f \sin\theta, \: f \cos\theta \big\rangle \end{align*}

Next, the fundamental vector product is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_x \times \mathbf{r}'_\theta &= \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & f' \cos\theta & f' \sin\theta \\ 0 & -f \sin\theta & f \cos\theta \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \bigg\langle \begin{vmatrix} f' \cos\theta & f' \sin\theta \\ -f \sin\theta & f \cos\theta \end{vmatrix}, \: -\begin{vmatrix} 1 & f' \sin\theta \\ 0 & f \cos\theta \end{vmatrix}, \: \begin{vmatrix} 1 & f' \cos\theta \\ 0 & -f \sin\theta \end{vmatrix} \bigg\rangle \\[5pt] &= \big\langle ff'\cos^2\theta+ff'\sin^2\theta, \: -f \cos\theta, \: -f\sin\theta \big\rangle \\[5pt] &= \big\langle ff', \: -f \cos\theta, \: -f\sin\theta \big\rangle. \end{align*}

Since $f=x^2,$ we obtain $f' = 2x.$ So, finally, we conclude that the fundamental vector product is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_x \times \mathbf{r}'_\theta = \big\langle {\color{blue}2x^3}, \: -x^2 \cos\theta, \: -x^2\sin\theta \big\rangle. \end{align*}

example.title: The Fundamental Vector Product of a Surface of Revolution

question.text:
\[ \big\langle \: \sqrt{z-1}\sin{\theta} \,, \: \sqrt{z-1} \cos {\theta} \,, \: \text{_______} \big\rangle \]

The fundamental vector product of the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $y=\sqrt{z-1}$ by $2\pi$ radians about the $z$-axis for $z \in [1,10]$ is given above. What is the $3$rd component of the product?
question.explanation:
Notice that $y=\sqrt{z-1} \geq 0$ for all $z \in [1,10].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r} = \big\langle f(z) \sin\theta, f(z) \cos\theta, \: z\big\rangle, \qquad (z,\theta) \in D \end{align*}

where $f(z)=\sqrt{z-1},$ and

\[ D = \big\{ (z,\theta) \: : \: 1 \leq z \leq 10, \: 0 \leq \theta \lt 2\pi \big\}. \]

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_z &= \bigg\langle \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial z}, \: \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial z}, \: \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial z} \bigg\rangle = \big\langle f' \sin\theta, \: f' \cos\theta, \: 1 \big\rangle \\[10pt] \mathbf{r}'_\theta &= \bigg\langle \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial \theta}, \: \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial \theta}, \: \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial \theta} \bigg\rangle = \big\langle f \cos\theta, \: -f \sin\theta, \: 0 \big\rangle \end{align*}

Next, the fundamental vector product is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_z \times \mathbf{r}'_\theta &= \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ f' \sin\theta & f' \cos\theta & 1\\ f \cos\theta & -f \sin\theta & 0 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \bigg\langle \begin{vmatrix} f' \cos\theta & 1 \\ -f \sin\theta & 0 \end{vmatrix}, \:- \begin{vmatrix} f' \sin\theta & 1 \\ f \cos\theta &0\end{vmatrix}, \: \begin{vmatrix} f' \sin\theta & f'\cos{\theta} \\ f \cos\theta & - f\sin\theta \end{vmatrix} \bigg\rangle \\[5pt] &= \big\langle f\sin\theta, \: f\cos\theta, \: -f'f \sin^2\theta- f'f \cos^2\theta \big\rangle \\[5pt] &= \big\langle f\sin\theta , \: f\cos{\theta} , \: -f'f \big\rangle. \end{align*}

Since $f=\sqrt{z-1},$ we obtain $f' = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{z-1}}.$ So, finally, we conclude that the fundamental vector product is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_z \times \mathbf{r}'_\theta = \left\langle \sqrt{z-1}\sin{\theta}, \: \sqrt{z-1} \cos {\theta}, \: {\color{blue}-\dfrac{1}{2}}\right\rangle. \end{align*}

example.title: The Fundamental Vector Product of a Surface of Revolution

question.text:
\[ \big\langle \: \cos^2 y\cos{\theta}, \text{_______}\,, \: \cos^2 y\sin\theta \big\rangle \]

The fundamental vector product of the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $x=\cos^2 y$ by $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis for $y \in \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2} \right]$ is given above. What is the $2$nd component of the product?
question.explanation:
Notice that $x=\cos^2 y \geq 0$ for all $y \in \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2} \right].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r} = \big\langle f(y) \cos\theta, y, \: f(y) \sin\theta \big\rangle, \qquad (y,\theta) \in D \end{align*}

where $f(y)=\cos^2 y,$ and

\[ D = \big\{ (y,\theta) \: : \: -\dfrac{\pi}{2} \leq y \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \: 0 \leq \theta \lt 2\pi \big\}. \]

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_y &= \bigg\langle \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial y}, \: \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial y}, \: \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y} \bigg\rangle = \big\langle f' \cos\theta, \:1, \: f' \sin\theta \big\rangle \\[10pt] \mathbf{r}'_\theta &= \bigg\langle \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial \theta}, \: \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial \theta}, \: \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial \theta} \bigg\rangle = \big\langle -f \sin\theta, \: 0, \: f \cos\theta \big\rangle \end{align*}

Next, the fundamental vector product is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_y \times \mathbf{r}'_\theta &= \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ f' \cos\theta & 1 & f' \sin\theta \\ -f \sin\theta &0 & f \cos\theta \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \bigg\langle \begin{vmatrix} 1& f' \sin\theta \\ 0 & f \cos\theta \end{vmatrix}, \:- \begin{vmatrix} f' \cos\theta & f'\sin{\theta} \\ - f \sin\theta & f\cos\theta \end{vmatrix}, \: \begin{vmatrix} f' \cos\theta & 1 \\ -f \sin\theta & 0 \end{vmatrix} \bigg\rangle \\[5pt] &= \big\langle f\cos\theta, \: -f'f \cos^2\theta- f'f \sin^2\theta, \: f\sin\theta \big\rangle \\[5pt] &= \big\langle f\cos{\theta}, \: -f'f , \: f\sin\theta \big\rangle. \end{align*}

Since $f=\cos^2 y,$ we obtain $f' = -2\sin y\cos y .$ So, finally, we conclude that the fundamental vector product is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_y \times \mathbf{r}'_\theta = \big\langle \cos^2 y\cos{\theta}, \: {\color{blue}2\sin y\cos^3 y}, \: \cos^2 y\sin\theta \big\rangle. \end{align*}

question.text:
\[ \big\langle \:-(z-z^2)\cos{\theta} \,, \: -(z-z^2) \sin {\theta} \,, \: \text{_______} \big\rangle \]

The fundamental vector product of the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $x=z-z^2$ by $2\pi$ radians about the $z$-axis for $z \in [0,1]$ is given above. What is the $3$rd component of the product?
question.explanation:
Notice that $x=z-z^2 \geq 0$ for all $z \in [0,1].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r} = \big\langle f(z) \cos\theta, f(z) \sin\theta, \: z\big\rangle, \qquad (z,\theta) \in D \end{align*}

where $f(z)=z-z^2,$ and

\[ D = \big\{ (z,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq z \leq 1, \: 0 \leq \theta \lt 2\pi \big\}. \]

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_z &= \bigg\langle \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial z}, \: \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial z}, \: \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial z} \bigg\rangle = \big\langle f' \cos\theta, \: f' \sin\theta, \: 1 \big\rangle \\[10pt] \mathbf{r}'_\theta &= \bigg\langle \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial \theta}, \: \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial \theta}, \: \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial \theta} \bigg\rangle = \big\langle -f \sin\theta, \: f \cos\theta, \: 0 \big\rangle \end{align*}

Next, the fundamental vector product is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_z \times \mathbf{r}'_\theta &= \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ f' \cos\theta & f' \sin\theta & 1\\ -f \sin\theta & f \cos\theta & 0 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \bigg\langle \begin{vmatrix} f' \sin\theta & 1 \\ f \cos\theta & 0 \end{vmatrix}, \:- \begin{vmatrix} f' \cos\theta & 1 \\ - f \sin\theta &0\end{vmatrix}, \: \begin{vmatrix} f' \cos\theta & f' \sin\theta \\ -f \sin\theta & f \cos\theta \end{vmatrix} \bigg\rangle \\[5pt] &= \big\langle -f\cos\theta, \: -f\sin\theta, \: f'f \cos^2\theta+f'f \sin^2\theta \big\rangle \\[5pt] &= \big\langle -f\cos\theta , \: -f\sin{\theta} , \: f'f \big\rangle. \end{align*}

Since $f=z-z^2,$ we obtain $f' = 1-2z.$ So, finally, we conclude that the fundamental vector product is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_z \times \mathbf{r}'_\theta = \left\langle -(z-z^2)\cos{\theta}, \: -(z-z^2) \sin {\theta}, \: {\color{blue} z-3z^2+2z^3}\right\rangle. \end{align*}

question.text:
\[ \big\langle \text{_______}\,, \: -\tan{x} \cos\theta, \: -\tan{x}\sin\theta \big\rangle \]

The fundamental vector product of the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $y=\tan{x}$ by $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis for $x \in \Big[0,\dfrac{\pi}{4} \Big]$ is given above. What is the $1$st component of the product?

Notice that $y=\tan{x} \geq 0$ for all $x \in \Big[0,\dfrac{\pi}{4} \Big].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

where $f(x)=\tan{x},$ and

\[ D = \big\{ (x,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq \pi/4, \: 0 \leq \theta \lt 2\pi \big\}. \]

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_x &= \bigg\langle \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial x}, \: \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial x}, \: \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x} \bigg\rangle = \big\langle 1, \: f' \cos\theta, \: f' \sin\theta \big\rangle \\[10pt] \mathbf{r}'_\theta &= \bigg\langle \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial \theta}, \: \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial \theta}, \: \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial \theta} \bigg\rangle = \big\langle 0, \: -f \sin\theta, \: f \cos\theta \big\rangle \end{align*}

Next, the fundamental vector product is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_x \times \mathbf{r}'_\theta &= \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & f' \cos\theta & f' \sin\theta \\ 0 & -f \sin\theta & f \cos\theta \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \bigg\langle \begin{vmatrix} f' \cos\theta & f' \sin\theta \\ -f \sin\theta & f \cos\theta \end{vmatrix}, \: -\begin{vmatrix} 1 & f' \sin\theta \\ 0 & f \cos\theta \end{vmatrix}, \: \begin{vmatrix} 1 & f' \cos\theta \\ 0 & -f \sin\theta \end{vmatrix} \bigg\rangle \\[5pt] &= \big\langle ff'\cos^2\theta+ff'\sin^2\theta, \: -f \cos\theta, \: -f\sin\theta \big\rangle \\[5pt] &= \big\langle ff', \: -f \cos\theta, \: -f\sin\theta \big\rangle. \end{align*}

Since $f=\tan{x},$ we obtain $f' = \sec^2{x}.$ So, finally, we conclude that the fundamental vector product is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_x \times \mathbf{r}'_\theta = \big\langle {\color{blue}\tan{x}\sec^2{x}}, \: -\tan{x} \cos\theta, \: -\tan{x}\sin\theta \big\rangle. \end{align*}

example.title: The Fundamental Vector Product of a Surface of Revolution
